question: Sorry, but I don’t think that’s the primary reason MCP was introduced. What you’re describing has already been addressed by architectural patterns that are often more efficient for that specific purpose. In my view, the real value of MCP is different: it hides deterministic implementation details from a probabilistic system—the LLM-based agent. What do I mean by deterministic implementation details? Exactly the things you mentioned: authentication, secret management, error handling, retries, API-specific behavior, rate limiting, and similar concerns. Those should remain encapsulated inside the MCP server. Instead, the agent is exposed to a set of simple, self-explanatory capabilities (or “skills”) that it can easily understand, compose, and orchestrate into workflows. The agent focuses on deciding what needs to be done, while the MCP implementation takes care of how it is done. So I don’t see MCP as a replacement for APIs. Rather, it acts as an abstraction layer (or proxy) that wraps APIs and presents them to the agent in a way that is natural for an LLM to use. Of course, that’s just my understanding of the concept. I may be wrong. Have a nice day!
